# A Deep Learning Framework for Predicting Teprotumumab Treatment Response in Thyroid Eye Disease

**Authors:** Saul Langarica; Nahyoung Grace Lee; Adham M Alkhadrawi; Young-Tak Kim; Sierra K Ha; Synho Do; Lisa Y Lin

**Affiliations:** 1Lab of Medical Imaging and Computation, Department of Radiology, Massachusetts General Hospital, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 2Department of Electrical Engineering, Pontificia Universidad Católica de Chile, Santiago, Chile | 3Ophthalmic Plastic Surgery Service, Department of Ophthalmology, Massachusetts Eye and Ear, Harvard Medical School, Boston, Massachusetts | 4KU-KIST Graduate School of Converging Science and Technology, Korea University, Seoul, South Korea | 5Kempner Institute, Harvard University, Boston, Massachusetts

## Abstract

To develop and evaluate a deep learning–based framework for quantifying thyroid eye disease (TED) severity before and after teprotumumab treatment, an insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor inhibitor, and to create a predictive model for forecasting individual patient responses to therapy.

A retrospective cohort study was conducted at a single institution, utilizing an image-based deep learning TED severity quantification model and a regression-based prediction model for teprotumumab treatment response.

One hundred eighty-four patients with a clinical diagnosis of TED and 44 individuals with normal orbital anatomy (controls) used for model training and validation. Additionally, 19 patients with pretreatment and posttreatment imaging were analyzed for treatment response.

A deep learning classification model integrating computed tomography-based orbital volumetric features and clinical data were developed to classify TED severity (normal, mild, and severe). A severity scoring model converted classification probabilities into a continuous severity metric. A regression-based model then predicted posttreatment severity using pretreatment clinical and imaging variables. Model performance was evaluated using accuracy, area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), root mean squared error, and coefficient of determination (R2).

Thyroid eye disease severity scores and predicted treatment response.

The classification model achieved an accuracy of 0.81 and an AUC of 0.88 in the primary cohort and an accuracy of 0.81 with an AUC of 0.86 in the treatment response cohort. Within the treatment response group (n = 19), a mean improvement of 0.194 severity points (P < 0.001) was observed after teprotumumab. The regression-based prediction model achieved a root mean squared error of 0.117 and an R2 of 0.82 in leave-one-out cross-validation and showed 89% concordance with clinician-assessed improvement.

This deep learning framework demonstrates promising performance for objective TED severity quantification and exploratory prediction of teprotumumab treatment response. By integrating clinical and imaging data, this approach provides a proof-of-concept for data-driven tools that may support individualized treatment planning in TED.

Keywords: Teprotumumab treatment, Deep learning, Thyroid eye disease, Predictive model

Thyroid eye disease (TED), also known as Graves' orbitopathy, is a complex autoimmune disorder characterized by orbital inflammation, adipose expansion, and extraocular muscle enlargement, often resulting in proptosis, diplopia, and, in severe cases, compressive optic neuropathy.1,2 The disease exhibits a heterogeneous clinical course, with some patients achieving spontaneous remission while others experience progressive and vision-threatening disease.2,3

Teprotumumab, a monoclonal antibody targeting the insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor, is the first US Food and Drug Administration-approved treatment for TED.4 Although teprotumumab has demonstrated considerable efficacy in mitigating symptoms such as proptosis and diplopia, treatment responses vary widely, and some patients show limited or transient improvement.5 In addition, the high cost of the medication and the potential for adverse effects such as hyperglycemia and hearing loss6,7 underscore the importance of identifying which patients are most likely to benefit before treatment initiation. Developing reliable, objective predictors of response therefore represents a major unmet clinical need.

Traditional systems for assessing TED severity, such as the Clinical Activity Score (CAS), VISA (vision, inflammation, strabismus, appearance) classification, and the European Group on Graves' Orbitopathy criteria, rely heavily on subjective clinical examination and provide limited quantitative information.8 Imaging techniques including computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging allow precise visualization of orbital anatomy and inflammation, but their interpretation remains highly operator-dependent and time-consuming.9 Consequently, there is growing interest in data-driven approaches that can extract reproducible and clinically meaningful features from imaging studies to enhance TED diagnosis and management.10 Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in ophthalmology because of its ability to analyze large, complex imaging datasets rapidly, objectively, and at low incremental cost.11 In TED, AI-based imaging analysis has shown promise for improving diagnostic accuracy, standardizing disease classification, and enabling more personalized treatment strategies.10,12,13 Studies using deep learning models such as convolutional neural networks and U-Net architectures have demonstrated strong performance in tasks including automated segmentation of orbital structures, disease activity assessment, and severity classification.13,14 However, most existing studies remain cross-sectional, focus on single-modality imaging, and do not extend to treatment prediction, highlighting an important gap between diagnostic modeling and therapeutic decision support.10

Building on our prior work in automated orbital segmentation and volumetric analysis for TED,15 the present study introduces a deep learning framework designed to address this gap. The framework comprises 3 sequential components: (1) a classification model integrating clinical and radiologic features extracted from a pretrained orbital segmentation network; (2) a severity-scoring model that translates classification probabilities into a continuous quantitative measure of disease severity; and (3) a regression-based model that predicts posttreatment severity using only pretreatment data. Together, these components provide a proof-of-concept for objective, image-based quantification and individualized prediction of teprotumumab response, with the long-term goal of informing personalized management strategies in TED.

## Methods

### Study Design

A retrospective cohort study was conducted over a 12-year period (August 2011–2023) at Massachusetts Eye and Ear, a tertiary ophthalmic institution. The study was approved by the Massachusetts General Brigham Institutional Review Board, and the need for written informed consent was waived. The study was conducted following the ethical standards outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki and in compliance with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act.

The primary objective of this study was to develop an objective, deep learning–based framework for quantifying TED severity and predicting individual responses to teprotumumab therapy. To achieve this, 3 interrelated models were developed: (1) a TED classification model to differentiate between normal (no TED), mild TED (without optic neuropathy), and severe TED cases (with optic neuropathy); (2) a TED severity scoring model that provides an objective and quantitative measure of disease severity by leveraging the classification model's predicted probabilities; and (3) a TED treatment response model that uses the calculated severity scores to predict how individual patients will respond to teprotumumab. An overview of these models is presented in Figure 1.

C, Thyroid eye disease treatment response model to predict post-teprotumumab severity scores. CT = computed tomography.*

The study included patients aged ≥18 years with a clinical diagnosis of TED who had undergone an orbital CT scan and a comprehensive examination by an oculoplastic surgeon within 3 months of imaging. Exclusion criteria included patients with other orbital conditions, such as trauma, tumors, or inflammatory diseases, as well as those with a history of prior orbital surgeries, including orbital decompression. Clinical and imaging data collection protocols were consistent among providers throughout the 12-year study period.

Patients were divided into 2 cohorts based on their treatment status. The classification cohort consisted of TED patients who had not undergone teprotumumab therapy and was used to develop the TED classification model. To enhance classification accuracy, this cohort was supplemented with a control group of individuals with normal orbital CT scans and no history of orbital disease. This dataset allowed for the differentiation between normal, mild, and severe TED cases. The treatment response cohort, comprised of patients who had completed a full course of teprotumumab therapy, was used for the development of the TED severity scoring and treatment response models. To be included in this cohort, patients were required to have a pretreatment orbital CT scan obtained within 12 months before initiating therapy and a posttreatment clinical examination conducted within 1 year of completing treatment.

Disease severity was determined through retrospective chart review. Severe TED was defined by the presence of any signs of optic neuropathy. Mild TED included patients with orbital signs or symptoms but without optic nerve involvement. Although the mild group was heterogeneous, this threshold provided an objective distinction between mild and severe diseases. Treatment response was defined by retrospective review of clinician documentation of improvement or stability in disease signs or symptoms after teprotumumab. Clinician assessments, which were also used for comparison with AI-derived results, refer to evaluations performed by the treating oculoplastic surgeon, typically before treatment initiation, once during therapy, and at treatment completion, with subsequent follow-ups individualized according to patient needs.

By leveraging these distinct patient cohorts and data sources, this study introduces a novel, data-driven approach to objectively assessing TED severity and predicting treatment response. These models have the potential to improve personalized clinical decision-making and optimize resource allocation in TED management.

### TED Classification Model Development

To extract image features used by the classification model, orbital CT images were preprocessed following the pipeline established in our prior work.15 Each scan (0.625-mm slice thickness, 512 × 512 pixels, window level = 1000 HU, window width = 350 HU) was normalized and cropped to isolate each orbit within a fixed 140 × 140 × 140 voxel region of interest.

Segmentation of orbital tissues was performed using a 2-dimensional U-Net architecture with an encoder–decoder design and a pretrained VGG16 encoder for feature extraction. The model was trained for 100 epochs using a learning rate of 1 × 10–4, a batch size of 4, and a cross-entropy loss function. The trained network implemented with PyTorch library, achieved Dice similarity coefficients of 0.902 for muscle segmentation and 0.921 for fat segmentation, confirming robust performance. The resulting segmentation masks were used to calculate extraocular muscle and orbital fat volumes for each orbit, which served as quantitative imaging features for downstream classification.

These imaging-derived features were combined with clinical and demographic variables, including gender, race, age, smoking history, Hertel exophthalmometry measurements, thyroid function tests, and thyroid antibody levels, to train a TED classification model that categorized each orbit as normal, mild TED, or severe TED. The classification cohort was randomly divided into training (70%) and validation (30%) subsets.

Two methodological challenges were addressed to ensure robust classification performance: class imbalance and feature selection. To handle class imbalance (see Table 1), 3 ensembles of binary classifiers were trained to distinguish among (1) normal vs not normal, (2) mild vs not mild, and (3) severe vs not severe orbits. Bootstrapped resampling of the majority (mild) class was used to create balanced subsets during training. For each ensemble, prediction probabilities from its component models were averaged, and each orbit was assigned to the class with the highest mean probability across ensembles (see Figure 2). This ensemble approach improved model stability and interpretability compared with a single multiclass classifier.

Feature selection was performed using Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO),16 a population-based stochastic optimization algorithm inspired by the collective behavior of flocks or swarms. In this framework, each “particle” represents a potential subset of features, and its position in the search space is iteratively updated based on both its own best performance and the global best observed among all particles. The optimization objective was to maximize the classification model's area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) on the validation set. This process identified the subset of imaging and clinical variables that contributed most significantly to model performance.

To interpret the trained models, Shapley Additive Explanations17 were used to quantify both the importance and directionality of each feature's contribution to classification outcomes. Shapley Additive Explanations is a post hoc explainability technique derived from game theory that attributes the model's predictions to individual feature effects (see Fig S1, available at www.ophthalmologyscience.org, to see the influence of each of selected variables by PSO in the classification models).

The final feature set selected by PSO was used to train the 3 Random Forest classifier ensembles. Each binary classifier within the ensemble was implemented using the Scikit-learn library and contained 200 decision trees. Default parameters were used for the remaining hyperparameters (Gini impurity criterion, bootstrapping enabled, and automatically determined maximum depth). Model performance was evaluated using fivefold cross-validation, with average accuracy and AUC calculated for each binary task. The ensemble's overall performance was computed by combining predictions from the 3 binary classifiers (normal vs not normal, mild vs not mild, and severe vs not severe) to assign the final class label to each orbit.

### TED Severity Score Development

To calculate the TED severity scores for each orbit, the trained classification model was leveraged. This score was determined by calculating the weighted Euclidean distance between an orbit's predicted class probabilities and those of a hypothetical “perfect” orbit (completely normal). To normalize the score within a range of 0 (completely normal) to 1 (most severe), the original value was scaled by the distance between the “perfect” hypothetical orbit and the “worst-case” orbit. As shown in Figure 3, each severity score is calculated per orbit as:

$$ s c o r e = α n o r m ( p h o n o r m – o n o r m ) 2 + α m i l d ( p h o m i l d – o m i l d ) 2 + α s e v e r e ( p h o s e v e r e – o s e v e r e ) 2 d max $$

With p h o being the probabilities of the “perfect” hypothetical orbit or of any orbit taken as a reference, o the inspected orbit, and d max the weighted Euclidean distance between the reference orbit and the “worst-case” orbit. The weights α were optimized to maximize class separability within the primary cohort, ensuring the score's clinical relevance.

*Figure 3: Formula for the calculation of TED severity score. TED = thyroid eye disease.*

Orbits from the treatment response cohort were then analyzed using this model to generate TED severity scores for both pretreatment and posttreatment states. The change in severity for each orbit was then quantified by calculating the difference between the pretreatment and posttreatment severity scores, providing a direct measure of the orbit's response to teprotumumab. This calculation is expressed as follows:

$$ t r e a t m e n t r e s p o n s e = s c o r e P r e – s c o r e P o s t $$

### TED Treatment Response Model Development

After assigning severity scores to each orbit pretreatment and posttreatment, a regression-based model was developed to predict an orbit's treatment response using pretreatment data alone. An ensemble of linear regression models was employed to estimate the post-teprotumumab severity score. Feature selection followed the same methodology as in the classification model. Selected features included pretreatment volumetric metrics from CT scans, clinical metadata, and classification model outputs such as pretreatment severity scores and class probabilities. Additionally, treatment-specific variables, including the duration of therapy, were incorporated to enhance predictive accuracy.

Given the limited sample size (n = 19), leave-one-out cross-validation18 was employed to ensure robust model evaluation, as this technique is particularly well-suited for small datasets, as this method maximizes data utilization while minimizing overfitting risk. In leave-one-out cross-validation, the model is trained repeatedly on all patients except one, which is held out for testing in each iteration, ensuring that every sample is used once for independent validation.

## Results

### TED Classification Model Results

The TED classification model was trained and validated using data from the classification cohort, which consisted of 456 orbits from 228 patients. In contrast, the treatment response cohort, comprising 19 patients with both pretreatment and posttreatment data, was used to further assess the model's performance. Patient demographics for both cohorts are summarized in Table 1.

Feature selection for the TED classification model began with 31 candidate variables, which were analyzed using PSO. The final set of selected features is detailed in Figure S1. Among these, muscle volume emerged as the most discriminative feature, with larger volumes strongly correlating with a higher likelihood of severe TED. Additionally, a history of smoking was significantly associated with an increased probability of severe TED classification. Although Hertel exophthalmometry values were initially included among the candidate clinical variables, they did not remain among the final selected predictors after optimization using PSO, likely due to high collinearity with imaging-derived orbital volume measures. The model thus relied primarily on volumetric CT features, which capture proptosis-related changes with greater anatomical precision.

After variable selection, the model achieved an average accuracy of 0.81 and an AUC of 0.88 across fivefold cross-validation, representing a notable improvement over the 0.69 accuracy and AUC of 0.72 observed with a single multiclass model. The individual performance of the binary classifiers within the classification cohort is illustrated in Figure 4A, with AUC values of 0.95 for normal vs not normal, 0.77 for mild vs not mild, and 0.88 for severe vs not severe. Notably, a similar performance was observed in the treatment response cohort (accuracy of 0.81 and AUC of 0.86), underscoring the generalizability and robustness of the classification model across different patient populations (see Fig 4).

*Figure 4: Receiver operating characteristic curves for the classification model in (A) the classification cohort and (B) the treatment response cohort. AUC = area under the receiver operating characteristic curve.*

To further evaluate model behavior, we analyzed the subset of patients who exhibited different disease severity grades between the 2 orbits. Among the 226 patients in the classification cohort, 12 (5.3%) demonstrated asymmetric TED diagnoses, typically with 1 orbit classified as mild and the other as severe. The model correctly identified both orbital classes in 7 of these 12 cases (58%). This reduced performance compared with the overall cohort likely reflects that several selected predictors, such as demographic and serologic variables, are patient-level rather than orbit-specific. Consequently, features shared between both orbits may limit the model's ability to capture subtle interorbital variation in disease severity. Future iterations incorporating additional orbit-level clinical features may enhance sensitivity to asymmetric presentations.

### TED Severity Score Results

The TED severity score was utilized to assign a quantitative and intuitive measure of TED severity to each orbit on a normalized scale from 0 (normal) to 1 (most severe). A total of 19 patients with both pre-teprotumumab and post-teprotumumab CT scans were included in the analysis to assess changes in severity after treatment. For pretreatment orbits, the cohort had an average severity score of 0.614 with a standard deviation of 0.186. After treatment, the posttreatment severity score decreased to an average of 0.420 with a standard deviation of 0.236. This corresponds to an average improvement of 0.194, representing a statistically significant reduction in TED severity (P = 1.7 × 10–4). The distribution of severity scores before and after treatment is illustrated in Figure 5A.

*Figure 5: A, Distribution of TED severity scores before and after treatment with teprotumumab. B, Distribution of model-predicted post-teprotumumab severity scores. TED = thyroid eye disease.*

### TED Treatment Response Results

The TED treatment response model was developed as an exploratory regression framework to estimate posttreatment severity scores based on pretreatment severity scores, imaging features, and clinical variables. After feature selection and optimization using PSO, the most relevant predictors of treatment response are presented in Figure S2 (available at www.ophthalmologyscience.org). Among these, the “severe” and “mild” class probabilities from the TED classification model were identified as key factors, but with opposite effects: a higher probability of severe TED in the pretreatment state was associated with greater improvement, while a higher probability of mild TED correlated with less improvement after treatment. This finding aligns with clinical expectations and current literature,19 as patients with more severe disease at baseline have greater potential for improvement when treated.

Consistent with findings from the classification model, a history of smoking was identified as a negative predictor of treatment response, further highlighting its detrimental impact on TED progression and therapeutic outcomes. In contrast, longer treatment duration showed a positive correlation with greater improvement, with patients exhibiting an improvement of >0.1 severity points having a median treatment duration of 175 days, compared with 149 days for those with <0.1 improvement. While this observation suggests a potential relationship between treatment duration and response, further investigation is needed to determine whether this reflects a true causal effect or is influenced by underlying data biases.

The model was evaluated using data from the treatment response cohort, which included 19 patients with both pretreatment and posttreatment information. Using leave-one-out cross-validation, it achieved a root mean squared error of 0.117 and an R2 score of 0.82, demonstrating strong predictive performance.

As illustrated in Figure 5B, the predicted posttreatment severity scores closely matched the actual observed distribution, with the differences being statistically indistinguishable (P = 0.940). Similarly, Figure 6 demonstrates alignment between predicted and actual orbit-level outcomes, showing that the framework is able to effectively estimate posttreatment trends. The solid line represents actual pretreatment and posttreatment scores determined by the TED severity model, while the lighter line depicts the predicted response from the TED treatment response model. The model effectively classified TED severity and was closely aligned with ground truth in most cases.

*Figure 6: Treatment response prediction vs actual treatment response at patient level using the treatment response cohort. TED = thyroid eye disease.*

### Validation of the TED Treatment Response Model against Clinician Assessment

Because posttreatment CT scans are not routinely performed in clinical practice, we used clinical evaluations as a surrogate ground truth to assess the model's performance from a different perspective. This approach closely reflects clinical decision-making, where treatment outcomes are primarily judged by clinical observation rather than imaging.

To validate the model in this way, we employed 2 distinct methods. First, we analyzed clinical reports, assigning a binary label of “1” if the clinician reported improvement and “0” otherwise. Because most clinical reports do not provide orbit-specific details, we determined the predicted class for each patient by calculating the average predicted improvement of both orbits. A positive average improvement was classified as “1” (indicating improvement), whereas a negative or zero average improvement was classified as “0” (indicating no improvement).

The performance metrics of our model, compared to clinician assessments, are summarized in Table 2. Our findings indicate a high concordance between the model's predictions and clinician-reported outcomes, reinforcing the potential clinical utility of this approach. It is important to note that metrics such as AUC could not be computed, as the model does not directly output class probabilities.

In addition to clinician reports, we examined the correlation between our model's continuous severity metric and changes in the CAS as a secondary validation measure. While CAS is widely used for assessing TED activity, it is known for its inherent subjectivity and interobserver variability, which limit its reliability in measuring disease severity.20 Nevertheless, we hypothesized that changes in CAS would correlate with our objective severity metric, reflecting clinicians' overall assessment of treatment response.

As depicted in Figure 7, we observed a modest positive correlation (r = 0.371) between predicted improvement using our model and improvement based on CAS. Although this relationship suggests that both measures capture related aspects of disease improvement, it should be interpreted as complementary rather than confirmatory evidence of the model's clinical validity.

## Discussion

This study presents a deep learning framework designed to utilize pre-teprotumumab clinical and radiographic data to predict individual treatment responses in patients with TED. To our knowledge, this is the first study to integrate pretreatment imaging and clinical data into a deep learning framework to explore individualized prediction of teprotumumab response in TED. While the algorithm is not designed specifically for anti-insulin-like growth factor-1 receptor mechanisms, it demonstrates the feasibility of using combined radiographic and clinical data to anticipate therapeutic outcomes.

Our study developed 3 learning-based models: the TED classification model, the TED severity model, and the TED treatment response model. The TED classification model, an enhancement of previous work by our group,15 effectively leveraged orbital CT volumetric data and patient meta-data to classify individual orbits into no TED, mild TED, or severe TED with optic neuropathy. The model demonstrated strong performance, achieving an average accuracy of 0.81 and an AUC of 0.88 across fivefold cross-validation. Feature selection analysis identified muscle volume as the most discriminative variable in classification, with higher muscle volume strongly correlating with severe TED. Additionally, elevated thyroid stimulating immunoglobulin levels and a history of smoking were also significant predictors of severe TED, further reinforcing their role in disease severity.

The TED severity model was developed by standardizing the range of cohort data, establishing a continuous severity spectrum from the most normal to the most severe orbit. This approach allowed for each orbit to be assigned an individualized severity score, providing a more granular and objective assessment of disease severity. Traditional methods for evaluating TED activity and severity, such as the CAS, VISA (vision, inflammation, strabismus, and appearance) classification, and the European Group of Graves' Orbitopathy classifications, rely heavily on subjective clinical assessments and may not fully capture the complexity of disease progression.8,21 Furthermore, these conventional approaches often fail to detect subtle changes over time and are ineffective in predicting treatment response, highlighting the need for more precise and objective metrics.22

To address these limitations, the TED severity model integrated a comprehensive range of clinical and radiographic data, including demographics, oculoplastic examination findings, laboratory values, and volumetric imaging data. By incorporating these diverse variables, the model generates a single severity score, enabling more precise tracking of disease progression and treatment-related changes in this heterogeneous disease. Using this score, we could determine that in our cohort, the majority of patients exhibited improvement in disease severity after treatment.

Building on the TED severity model's outcomes, we developed the TED treatment response model as an exploratory regression framework that leverages longitudinal data to estimate posttreatment severity scores using pretreatment clinical and radiographic data. This model provides individualized predictions of whether a patient is likely to experience improvement, worsening, or no significant change in TED severity after teprotumumab therapy. Feature analysis of the model revealed that patients with more severe disease at baseline were more likely to exhibit greater treatment response, whereas a history of smoking (current or former) was associated with poorer therapeutic outcomes. These observations align with established TED risk factors; however, given the limited sample size, further studies with larger cohorts are required to determine whether this influence represents a truly predictive effect or merely an associative relationship.

Predictions of treatment response showed good agreement with clinician assessments, and a positive correlation was observed between the model's predicted response and changes in the CAS documented in medical charts. These results suggest that the proposed framework may help estimate treatment response trends and identify patients who could be more likely to benefit from teprotumumab therapy. While preliminary, the consistent performance across cross-validation folds supports the model's internal stability. Nonetheless, given the limited sample size, sensitivity analysis and external validation will be essential in future studies to confirm generalizability and predictive reliability.

Over the past decade, deep learning models have been increasingly utilized to predict individual patient responses to treatment across various medical fields. As clinical medicine continues to shift toward precision medicine, these models offer a powerful tool for identifying complex associations that traditional statistical methods may overlook.23

In oncology, which is at the forefront of precision medicine, numerous AI and deep learning–based models have been developed to integrate clinical, radiographic, and genomic data to predict tumor responses to various treatments.20,24,25 Similarly, in neurology, deep learning has been applied to predict treatment response to antiseizure medications in patients with newly diagnosed epilepsy. One study incorporated clinical factors, electroencephalography findings, and imaging data to forecast treatment success across 7 different antiseizure medications, providing a potential decision-support tool for clinicians and reducing reliance on the traditional trial-and-error approach.26

Recent advances in quantitative imaging have highlighted the value of orbital volume analysis and radiologic biomarkers in understanding TED activity and treatment outcomes. Quantitative magnetic resonance imaging and CT studies have demonstrated strong correlations between extraocular muscle and fat volumes and clinical disease activity. For example, Ugradar et al19 conducted a prospective longitudinal study of 35 patients treated with teprotumumab and applied multivariate regression using manually derived volumetric measurements to identify baseline predictors of proptosis response, including muscle volume and proptosis. Other imaging-based machine-learning and radiomic studies have explored steroid or tocilizumab response prediction,22,27,28 collectively demonstrating the emerging role of imaging biomarkers in TED management.

Building on this growing field, our study provides a proof-of-concept for applying learning models to predict treatment response in TED. By integrating clinical and radiographic pretreatment data, the model demonstrates the potential to inform personalized TED management and to estimate the likelihood of treatment response. While preliminary, such predictive modeling may assist in guiding clinical decision-making, improving patient counseling, and supporting future development of data-driven treatment selection tools as additional TED therapies emerge.

A key strength of this study is its use of learning algorithms to integrate different sources of clinical and radiographic data, providing an objective and data-driven prediction of treatment response. However, several limitations should be considered. First, the use of clinician-reported improvement as a surrogate ground truth is consistent with clinical practice but introduces inherent subjectivity that may affect model precision. Because clinical documentation was not orbit-specific and may vary by examiner or timing, this variability could contribute to residual noise in model predictions. Nevertheless, the strong agreement between model-predicted and clinician-reported outcomes (89% accuracy) suggests that the algorithm effectively captures clinically meaningful treatment trends. Future studies incorporating standardized, orbit-level disease-activity scores or objective imaging endpoints could further improve predictive accuracy and reduce subjectivity-related variability. Second, the model was trained on a relatively small cohort of patients. Due to the limited availability of posttreatment orbital CT scans, only a subset of patients was available for training in the treatment response prediction model. This constrained the statistical power of the analysis and increased the potential risk of overfitting, as the model may have captured sample-specific rather than generalizable patterns. Although fivefold and leave-one-out cross-validation were implemented to mitigate this risk, external validation on larger, independent datasets will be essential to confirm the model's reproducibility and predictive reliability.

Additionally, as this was a retrospective study, pretreatment and posttreatment clinical examinations and imaging studies were not collected at uniform time points, introducing some heterogeneity in model training and potential confounding effects. However, this variability reflects clinical practice, where treatment initiation timing varies based on individual patient disease progression and provider decision-making. Another limitation is that the study was conducted at a single institution, potentially reducing the heterogeneity of the training dataset and leading to model overfitting. Furthermore, the segmentation model quantified total extraocular muscle volume rather than individual rectus muscle volumes; incorporating muscle-specific volumetric data in future models may enhance sensitivity to regional disease patterns and improve predictive performance. Future studies with larger, multi-institutional datasets and prospective validation will be necessary to further refine this approach and optimize its clinical accuracy and generalizability before widespread clinical implementation.

Thyroid eye disease is a highly heterogeneous disease, with multiple contributing factors influencing disease severity and treatment response. Determining which patients will benefit most from specific treatments remains a clinical challenge. By integrating both clinical and radiographic features, the AI models presented in this work can provide a more objective assessment of TED severity and predict individual responses to teprotumumab therapy. As medical care continues to evolve toward personalized and precision-based treatment strategies, models like this may serve as valuable decision-support tools in determining optimal treatment pathways for individual TED patients. Future advancements in AI-driven predictive modeling could further enhance treatment selection, patient counseling, and clinical outcomes, ultimately improving the management of TED and other complex autoimmune diseases.

## Conclusion

This study introduces a deep learning framework that offers an objective and personalized approach to managing TED by quantifying disease severity and predicting individual responses to teprotumumab. By integrating clinical and radiographic data, our models provide a data-driven alternative to traditional, more subjective assessment methods, potentially improving treatment selection and patient outcomes. The predictive capabilities of this approach suggest that AI can play a valuable role in precision medicine, helping clinicians make more informed decisions while optimizing the allocation of health care resources.

Despite promising results, the study also highlights the challenges of AI implementation in clinical practice, including the need for larger, multicenter validation studies to enhance model generalizability. As more treatments for TED become available, models like this could be expanded to guide comparative treatment selection, ensuring that patients receive the most effective and personalized care. Moving forward, integrating AI-driven prediction models into routine clinical workflows has the potential to transform TED management, advancing the field toward a more objective, efficient, and patient-specific approach to treatment.
